faq.question: What is Readerfold?
faq.answer: Readerfold is a panel of AI beta readers for fiction writers, designed to simulate how different people might experience a story. Up to five readers bring distinct tastes, voices, and perspectives. Follow their reactions beside the passages that prompted them, compare where they connect or disagree, and use the editorial report to consider your next revision.

faq.question: How does an AI beta reader work?
faq.answer: An AI beta reader uses a language model to simulate a reader’s experience of a story. In Readerfold, each reader has generated tastes, reading habits, and a voice. You can choose a focus for each reader, such as character connection or plot logic, and compare their curiosity, expectations, confusion, and interpretations as they read.

faq.question: What makes Readerfold’s reading experience distinctive?
faq.answer: Readerfold centers the individual reader’s reaction: what draws them in, how they interpret a character, and where they hesitate or change their expectations. Different AI readers respond to the same manuscript in their own voices, so you can compare perspectives before reviewing the combined editorial report. Their reactions are simulations, not feedback from real people or a prediction of audience response.

faq.question: Can AI feedback replace human beta readers or an editor?
faq.answer: AI feedback can help you explore a draft before sharing it with people. It can also miss context, misunderstand your intent, or give conflicting advice. Human beta readers bring lived experience, and professional editors bring judgment that an AI panel cannot guarantee. You decide which suggestions serve your story.

faq.question: What can I upload?
faq.answer: You can paste your writing or upload a TXT, DOCX, or PDF file. Confirm the extracted text, genre, and intended audience before starting a reading.

faq.question: Can I try Readerfold for free?
faq.answer: You can create an account and try Readerfold with free starter credits without a payment card. Credit use varies with manuscript length, reader setup, panel size, and additional reports. The Pricing page explains the current allowances and paid options.

faq.question: Will my manuscript be used to train AI?
faq.answer: Readerfold does not use your manuscript to train AI models, and we have opted out of training with our AI providers. We send relevant manuscript text to those providers to generate analysis and feedback. Training opt-outs do not mean zero retention; the Privacy policy explains provider processing and storage.

faq.question: Will my manuscript be published or shared publicly?
faq.answer: No. Uploading to Readerfold does not publish your manuscript or make your feedback public. You keep your rights to your writing, and we do not acquire publishing rights or permission to use it in public marketing. Relevant content is processed by the service providers described in our Privacy policy.

faq.question: Do you store my manuscript, and can I delete it?
faq.answer: Yes. Readerfold saves your manuscript and feedback in your account so you can return to them. You can delete a manuscript or contact support to request deletion. Active readings must finish before manuscript deletion. Deletion may not immediately remove backup copies, and external providers follow their own retention arrangements. See the Privacy policy for details and account deletion requests.

/beta-readers.heading: Beta readers help you see the story your audience receives.
/beta-readers.intro: A beta reader reads a draft from the audience's point of view and tells you where the story engages, confuses, surprises, or loses them. Writers usually seek beta feedback after completing a workable draft but before final proofreading or publication.

sections.heading: What does a beta reader do?
sections.text: A beta reader responds to the reading experience rather than correcting every sentence. Useful feedback may identify where attention drops, a character's decision feels unconvincing, a reveal lacks setup, or important context arrives too late. Beta readers do not replace copyeditors, proofreaders, sensitivity readers, or professional editors; each role answers different questions.

sections.heading: When should you ask for beta reader feedback?
sections.text: Share a draft when its beginning, middle, and ending are present and you are ready to reconsider substantial choices. If you already know that scenes are missing or the ending will change, revise those issues first. Beta feedback is most useful when readers can experience the intended story and you still have room to act on what they notice.

sections.heading: How do you find beta readers for free?
sections.text: Look for readers who already enjoy your genre through critique swaps, writing groups, library writing circles, or communities that allow beta requests. Introduce the genre, word count, draft stage, content notes, and feedback you want. Agree on scope and timing before sending a file; a short sample can help both sides check the fit. If you offer a swap, be clear about the time you can give in return. Community rules differ, so check them before posting or sharing AI-generated material.

sections.heading: What should you ask beta readers?
sections.text: Ask a small set of questions tied to the experience you want to create: Where did you want to keep reading? Where were you confused? Which character choices felt earned or unearned? When did the pace feel rushed or slow? What did you expect would happen next? Open questions usually reveal more than asking whether the book was good.

sections.heading: Human and AI beta readers offer different perspectives
sections.text: Human beta readers bring lived experience, taste, genre knowledge, and genuine emotional response. AI beta readers can provide fast, repeatable reactions focused on particular craft questions, but they can misunderstand context, invent problems, or share the same model bias. AI feedback works best as an exploratory step before or alongside feedback from people, not as evidence of how a real audience will respond.

sections.heading: How do you use conflicting feedback?
sections.text: Treat feedback as evidence about a reader's experience, not an instruction to make every suggested change. Return to the passage behind each reaction, look for patterns, and compare them with your intended audience and purpose. When readers disagree, decide which response is closer to the experience you want the story to create.

sections.heading: How Readerfold supports the beta reading process
sections.text: Readerfold gives fiction writers a private panel of AI beta readers designed to respond like people experiencing a story. Each brings distinct tastes and a voice. Compare what draws them in, how they interpret a character, and where they become uncertain, with reactions tied to your passages. Their responses can help you form revision questions before sharing the draft with human readers.

/ai-beta-reader.heading: AI readers with their own tastes, voices, and reactions.
/ai-beta-reader.intro: Readerfold is designed to simulate the experience of different people reading your fiction. Each AI beta reader brings distinct tastes, reading habits, and a voice. Follow what catches their attention, how they interpret a character, and where their expectations change, then compare their perspectives on the same passage.

sections.heading: What does a simulated reader reaction look like?
sections.text: A reader might say, “I want her to open the letter, but I am worried about what she will find.” Another might wonder why she has kept it sealed. These illustrative reactions describe curiosity and interpretation as the story unfolds. Readerfold connects reactions to the manuscript so you can examine the moment that prompted each response.

sections.heading: Why give AI beta readers different perspectives?
sections.text: The same detail can reassure one reader and make another suspicious. Distinct tastes and reading priorities give you different ways to explore a scene: one reader follows the emotional relationship, another anticipates the next reveal, and another questions a character’s reasoning. They may agree or disagree; neither outcome proves how a real audience will respond.

sections.heading: Ask a specific reading question
sections.text: Instead of asking whether your story is good, choose a question the draft can answer. Does the opening establish a reason to keep reading? Is the protagonist's choice understandable? Does a reveal arrive before the reader has enough context? Give different readers different priorities.

sections.heading: Read the passage behind the reaction
sections.text: A broad judgment is difficult to act on. Readerfold places reader reactions beside the manuscript so you can return to the words that prompted them. Compare an emotional reader's connection with an analytical reader's questions about structure and a skeptical reader's doubts about logic.

sections.heading: Use disagreement as a revision question
sections.text: If one reader enjoys uncertainty and another feels lost, that is a choice to examine. Revisit the intended audience and ask what readers need to know at this point. Agreement is not proof, and disagreement does not mean the passage is broken.

sections.heading: Bring human readers into the process
sections.text: An AI panel does not represent a real audience or predict sales. After exploring its feedback, share the revised draft with human beta readers who know your genre. For sensitive subject matter or publication decisions, seek people with relevant experience.

/manuscript-feedback.heading: Make manuscript feedback useful to your next revision.
/manuscript-feedback.intro: See how the same passage lands with different simulated readers. Readerfold’s AI beta readers bring distinct tastes and voices to your fiction, expressing curiosity, connection, and doubts beside your words. Compare their reactions first, then use the editorial report to consider what to revise.

sections.heading: Start with the draft's purpose
sections.text: Choose the genre and audience, then name the part of the reading experience you want to understand. An opening chapter may need a clear hook; a later chapter may need emotional continuity. Focus the reading on what you are ready to revise.

sections.heading: Separate structure from sentence work
sections.text: Look first at character goals, cause and effect, pacing, and missing context. Polishing a sentence before deciding whether the scene belongs can create avoidable work. Keep line-level observations for a later pass when the structure is settled.

sections.heading: Compare patterns in the editorial report
sections.text: Use Readerfold's editorial report to bring the panel's observations together. Return to the original passages before accepting a conclusion. Repeated confusion can identify a place to investigate, but several AI readers can still share the same mistaken assumption.

sections.heading: Revise one question at a time
sections.text: Choose a small number of changes with a clear purpose. For example: make the scene goal visible earlier, add the missing cause of a decision, or shorten the delay before a reveal. Re-read afterward and check whether the change serves your intended effect.
